title: SDK triage: resumable streaming, org token rotation, and cross-language auth ergonomics
creator: Marco Reyes
description:
Summary: Multiple enterprise customers (BankCo, HealthAI, and RetailHub) requested first-class SDK support for resumable streaming sessions combined with per-organization token rotation and SSO-friendly auth flows. This ticket triages the requests, documents constraints, proposes an MVP, and outlines a rollout plan across Python, Go, and Java SDKs.

Context & customer asks: Customers want the ability to: 1) resume long-running streaming sessions (chat/audio transcription/continuous inference) after transient network drops or client restarts; 2) rotate organization-scoped tokens without disrupting active sessions; and 3) integrate SAML/SAML2/OIDC SSO patterns in client libs so their platform engineers can standardize auth patterns. Several customers called this out in onboarding calls and one Enterprise ATO requires explicit session resume + auditability.

Constraints & non-goals: We must avoid adding heavy stateful server components in hosted mode for the initial MVP. Non-goal: building a full persistence-backed session broker. Non-goal: immediate parity for all language bindings — target MVP for Python and Go, lightweight shim/adapter for Java.

Design options considered:
- A: Server-side resume tokens + ephemeral session keys (stateless resume tokens encoded with HMAC). Pros: simple to implement, no server-side session store. Cons: limitation on session metadata size and harder to revoke mid-session without token revocation APIs.
- B: Minimal session-store (Redis) to support offset checkpointing and explicit resume pointers. Pros: robust, supports large session state (KV cache offsets). Cons: operational cost and complexity for hosted; needs clear data retention policies for Private deployments.
- C: Client-side checkpointing + replay (clients checkpoint offsets and resubmit diffs). Pros: zero server state. Cons: heavier client logic and brittle on model changes or KV cache invalidations.

Initial decision: Implement option A for the hosted API MVP (stateless resume tokens with versioned HMAC and short TTLs) combined with a documented migration path to option B if customers need stronger revocation/large-state support. For Private deployments we will offer an installer toggle to enable session-store backed resume (option B) with configurable retention and encryption at rest.

MVP scope & acceptance criteria:
- SDK surface: add StreamingSession class exposing resume() and checkpoint() in Python and Go. Methods must: return opaque resume token, allow resuming from token, and expose server backpressure hints.
- Auth ergonomics: SDKs must accept either API keys, short-lived org tokens, or a callback-based token provider to support SSO integrations without exposing credentials in memory.
- Rotation behavior: rotating tokens via the Console or KMS must not invalidate existing resume tokens for the TTL period; provide an admin API to revoke active sessions if required.
- Docs & examples: Confluence PRD, Python and Go example repos, and a migration guide for on-prem customers.
- Telemetry: add session events (session.started, session.checkpoint, session.resumed, session.revoked) to our telemetry schema with org_id and session_id tags.

Rollout plan:
- Discovery sprint (2 weeks): finalize token encoding spec, security review, and API contract.
- Engineering spike (2 weeks): PoC stateless resume tokens + Python SDK prototype.
- Parallel implementation (4 weeks): complete Python + Go; design Java shim API; update Console with session revocation control.
- Beta with 3 pilot customers (4 weeks): enable feature flags, collect QoE metrics and edge-case failures.
- GA in client-sdk-2026.06 release.

Risks & mitigation:
- Security: stateless tokens could be replayed if compromised. Mitigation: HMAC versioning, short TTLs, bind tokens to client fingerprint (IP/user-agent optional), and require admin revoke for longer exposure.
- Complexity across languages: differing networking models (async Python vs goroutines vs JVM threads). Mitigation: define clear async contract, provide sync and async helpers, and add integration tests per language.
- Customer trust: customers may demand stronger guarantees (complete revocation). Mitigation: Private deployment option with session store + audit logs; document differences clearly.

Next steps:
1) Schedule 60m design review with Security and Runtime (invite: Priya Nair, Jin Park, Matteo Russo) — target 2026-02-09.
2) Draft Confluence design doc: link below.
3) Create ENG spike tickets for python-sdk resume PoC and runtime token validation (ENG-34111, ENG-34112).
4) Add to Cycle 2026-W10 and assign owners.

Outcome desired: Reduce enterprise onboarding friction for streaming use-cases, enable secure token rotation with minimal disruption, and establish a cross-language pattern that scales to Dedicated/Private modes.
